c.tagline: Sudan's Red Sea port and gateway to the Sanganeb reef and the coral ruins of Suakin.

taxi.fareNote: There are no ride-hail apps in Port Sudan — agree the fare with the driver before setting off. Shared taxis and amjads (small three-wheeled rickshaws) handle short hops around town; carry small notes in cash.

emergency.note: 999 reaches the police and 333 the ambulance service. Sudan is affected by an ongoing civil conflict and Port Sudan currently serves as the country's de facto wartime administrative seat; check your government's travel advisories before any visit.

avoid.reason: Most governments advise against all travel to Sudan; avoid the port and military installations, which have been targeted by drone strikes.
Wartime conditions bring checkpoints, fuel and power shortages and drone-attack risk — keep a low profile and register with your embassy.

hood_desc: The commercial heart of the city around the main market (souq), government offices and the boardwalk overlooking the port; the practical, walkable base close to banks, cafés and most of the central hotels.
The seafront corniche facing the Red Sea, where fishermen work and locals stroll in the sea breeze; the scenic waterfront edge of the city with views over the harbour.

water.note: Drink bottled or treated water only.

transit.hours: Minibuses and shared taxis run mainly during daylight hours; after dark, chartered taxis and amjads are the main way to get around.
transit.note: Port Sudan has no formal public transport system; getting around means shared minibuses and taxis on the main roads, plus amjads (three-wheeled rickshaws) for short local hops.
transit.pay: Pay the driver or conductor directly in cash; there is no transit card, and with a heavily cash-based economy you should carry small notes. Fares are negotiated for private hires.

bus: Long-distance buses to Khartoum, Kassala & Atbara
ferry: Red Sea cargo & passenger links to Jeddah (Suakin/Port Sudan)

tip.r: Not obligatory; rounding up the bill or leaving a small amount for good service is appreciated but not expected.

landmarks: Umbria Wreck
This Italian freighter, scuttled in 1940 with bombs and Fiat cars still in her holds, is celebrated among the world's greatest wreck dives.
Shaab Rumi Reef and Precontinent II
Divers explore the underwater remains of Jacques Cousteau's 1963 Precontinent II habitat, sci-fi relics of humanity's first undersea village experiment.
Port Sudan Corniche
The palm-lined waterfront promenade surveys the busy harbor and Red Sea, liveliest at dusk when families stroll past faded colonial-era facades.
Souq El Kebir (Central Market)
Port Sudan's sprawling market perfumes the air with coffee, cardamom and frankincense as Beja tribesmen with distinctive swords trade alongside fishermen.
Arous Village
This abandoned beach resort, famously run as a Mossad front in the 1980s and inspiration for a Netflix film, stands on a lonely shore north of town.
Towartit Reefs
A maze of coral pillars and lagoons just offshore, these easily reached reefs give snorkelers their first taste of Sudan's underwater riches.
Red Sea University
Port Sudan's main public university, a sprawling campus that is also a recognizable landmark and gathering point in the city.
Red Sea Museum
A small museum near the harbor devoted to the Red Sea's marine life, with shell collections and displays on the coast's coral reefs.
Port Sudan Lighthouse
A working lighthouse on a headland above the harbor, offering views over the docks and the city's skyline.
Port Sudan Harbour
The country's principal deep-water port, a working waterfront where cargo ships and traditional wooden dhows load and unload side by side.

dom.op: Sudan Railways Corporation — tickets at Port Sudan station when services are running

train.note: Port Sudan is the eastern terminus of Sudan's 1,067 mm gauge network, with the line running inland through Haiya to Atbara and on to Khartoum. Passenger trains on it had already dwindled to occasional and unadvertised workings well before 2023 - the priority has long been container and fuel traffic from the port - and the civil war that began in April 2023 has left the network largely paralysed with track and rolling stock damaged. There has never been an international passenger train from Sudan; the Wadi Halfa line towards Egypt ends at the border and Egyptian metals begin separately at Aswan. Treat any rail journey here as an unpredictable local arrangement to be checked in person at the station.

bus.note: Long-distance coaches leave from the Port Sudan bus station for Khartoum (12-15 hours in normal times), Atbara, Kassala and Gedaref, with seats sold at the individual company offices in the terminal for cash rather than online. No scheduled international coach runs from Port Sudan: travellers bound for Egypt change at Wadi Halfa for the Argeen/Qustul crossing, and those heading to Ethiopia change at Gedaref for the Gallabat/Metema border, while the Eritrean frontier beyond Kassala is generally closed. Since April 2023 road travel across Sudan has been dangerous, checkpoints are numerous and routes change at short notice; most governments advise against all travel to the country.

intl.to: Jeddah (Saudi Arabia) - Red Sea crossing from Port Sudan and from the Suakin ferry terminal about 55 km south, 10-12 hr
intl.op: Namma Shipping Lines — tickets through port shipping agents

ferry.note: The Red Sea crossing to Jeddah is worked by Ro-Ro vehicle and passenger ships used mainly by pilgrims, traders and lorry drivers rather than tourists, sailing from Port Sudan itself and more often from the dedicated terminal at Suakin, an hour south by road. Departures are irregular at the best of times and have been repeatedly suspended, diverted or commandeered since the war began, when Port Sudan became the country's main evacuation and relief gateway. A Saudi visa must be held before boarding and tickets are arranged in person through a shipping agent, with vehicles booked several days ahead. Crossings take roughly 10-12 hours and conditions on board are basic.

half.blurb: Crumbling coral-stone ruins of a once-great Ottoman-era Red Sea trading port on an island lagoon, about 60 km south of the city.
half.name: Suakin
Suakin Old Town
half.blurb: An hour south, the crumbling coral-block palaces and mosques of this once-great Ottoman Red Sea port form one of Africa's most haunting ruins.

full.blurb: A UNESCO-listed atoll reef and colonial-era lighthouse offering some of the Red Sea's finest wall diving, reached by boat from the coast.
full.name: Sanganeb Marine National Park

full.blurb: A remote UNESCO marine reserve of coral reefs, dugongs, manta rays and mangroves around Mukkawar Island, north of the city.
full.name: Dungonab Bay & Mukkawar Island
Erkowit
full.blurb: A faded colonial-era hill station in the mist-catching Red Sea Hills, its cool green slopes once made it Sudan's unlikely honeymoon retreat.
